items.prompt: What is the digest's byte budget, and whataudits it?
options: ≤ 4,096 bytes — the digest prints its own size against the cap, and the budget is contract-tested
No cap — the digest is as long as the night was
items.explanation: The document audits its own budget: 3,412/4,096 in the discipline strip, and the cap is tested so a growing digest cannot quietly learn to summarise away its refusals. (obj-22-a)

items.prompt: Why do REFUSALS come first in the digest?
options: Because the operator with two minutes reads only section one — and an operator who reads only refusals still knows whether any safety boundary was approached; leading with successes buries the signal
items.explanation: Refusals-first is a SAFETY property — the first scroll is the audit; it is contract-tested, not a style choice. (obj-22-a)

items.prompt: From a digest header 'mode: sim · cadence: 63 min (measured)', what does the operator know?
options: The run used live fetches and exact timing
Mechanisms were exercised against fixtures (sim), and the observed interval was 63 minutes against a configured 60 — labels and measured jitter, both honesty devices
items.explanation: The mode label says which questions the numbers can answer; the measured cadence carries jitter — the earliest symptom of a struggling loop. (obj-22-b)

items.prompt: Which discipline-strip entry enumerates what the run could NOT measure?
options: the unmeasured list — every unmeasured quantity named with its n; the digest's confession posture and its most trustworthy feature
items.explanation: A system that never says unmeasured is either omniscient or lying: the list makes ignorance an artifact. (obj-22-b)
